```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = TRUE,
                     fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5, fig.align = "center",
                     dpi = 120, comment = "#>")
options(width = 90)
blue <- "#0072B2"
orange <- "#D55E00"
green <- "#009E73"
purple <- "#CC79A7"
B <- as.integer(params$simulation_reps)
stopifnot(length(B) == 1L, is.finite(B), B >= 20L)
# Direct Gaussian KDE for modest sample sizes.
kde <- function(x, grid, h) {
  stopifnot(length(x) > 1L, all(is.finite(x)),
            length(h) == 1L, is.finite(h), h > 0)
  rowMeans(dnorm(outer(grid, x, "-") / h)) / h
}
trapz <- function(x, y) sum(diff(x) * (head(y, -1) + tail(y, -1)) / 2)
# Keep local graphics settings local to each multi-panel example.
with_panels <- function(nr, nc, code) {
  old <- par(mfrow = c(nr, nc), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 1))
  on.exit(par(old))
  force(code)
}
```

# Learning goals and lesson route

This unit develops Kernel Density Estimation from individual observations, then separates the effects of **bandwidth** and **sample size**.

By the end, you should be able to:

- construct a KDE and identify the centre and mode of each Gaussian kernel;
- interpret density as probability per unit, with probability represented by area;
- distinguish changing bandwidth at fixed sample size from increasing sample size at fixed bandwidth;
- explain bias and variability using repeated samples;
- compare automatic bandwidth choices and recognise support problems.
- compare common kernels at a matched smoothing scale and explain why kernel
  choice is different from bandwidth choice.

**Prerequisites:** density, probability as area, mean and variance, and basic R. The asymptotic rate and cross-validation derivation are optional extensions.

**Unit route:** build a density from observations, explore bandwidth on real
waiting times, separate sample size from smoothing using known populations,
compare kernel shapes, and check whether the estimator respects the support.
Short activities appear where each idea is introduced: predict, plot, explain.

**Reproducibility.** Examples use base R and datasets shipped with R. No data
downloads or objects from other units are needed. Simulations have explicit
seeds.

- R documentation: [density](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/density.html) and [bandwidth selectors](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/bandwidth.html).

# KDE: build the curve before choosing the bandwidth

## From a histogram to overlapping contributions

A histogram aggregates observations in bins. KDE distributes a small amount of
density around every observation and adds the contributions.

The **bandwidth**, written $h$, is the positive number that controls the width
of each contribution. For a Gaussian kernel, $h$ is exactly the standard
deviation of the normal curve centred at each observation. It has the same
units as the data: for waiting times in minutes, $h=5$ means a kernel standard
deviation of five minutes. It is not the standard deviation of the sample,
the spacing of the plotting grid, or the width of a histogram bin.

A smaller bandwidth gives narrower, taller contributions and preserves more
local detail, including random fluctuations. A larger bandwidth gives wider,
lower contributions and smooths over that detail. We first choose $h$ ourselves
to see its effect; later we study ways to choose it from the data.

With $n$ observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, the Gaussian KDE is

\[
\widehat f_h(x)=\frac{1}{nh}\sum_{i=1}^n
\phi\!\left(\frac{x-X_i}{h}\right),\qquad h>0,
\]

where $\phi$ is the standard normal density. The Gaussian kernel does **not** assume that the data have a normal distribution: the estimate is a mixture of many shifted kernels.

```{r individual-kernels, fig.height=5.5, fig.cap="Observed values are shown at y = 0. Each is vertically aligned with the mode of its own normal kernel; the thick blue curve is the sum of the contributions.", fig.alt="Eight observed points lie on the zero baseline. A highlighted point has a dashed vertical line to the peak of its own Gaussian contribution."}
x_small <- c(-1.7, -1.2, -.9, -.5, .4, .8, 1.0, 1.7)
h_small <- .35
g_small <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = 601)
contributions <- sapply(x_small, function(z)
  dnorm(g_small, mean = z, sd = h_small) / length(x_small))
total <- rowSums(contributions)
matplot(g_small, contributions, type = "l", lty = 1, col = "grey65",
        ylim = c(-.025, max(total) * 1.35),
        xlab = "Observed variable", ylab = "Density")
abline(h = 0, col = "grey75")
lines(g_small, total, col = blue, lwd = 3)
# Every observed value is plotted at exactly y = 0, not as a rug below the axis.
points(x_small, rep(0, length(x_small)), pch = 16, cex = 1.1)
# Highlight one observation, its contribution, and the common x coordinate.
i <- 5
peak_height <- dnorm(x_small[i], mean = x_small[i], sd = h_small) /
  length(x_small)
lines(g_small, contributions[, i], col = orange, lwd = 2)
segments(x_small[i], 0, x_small[i], peak_height, col = orange, lty = 2)
points(x_small[i], 0, pch = 16, col = orange, cex = 1.3)
points(x_small[i], peak_height, pch = 1, col = orange, cex = 1.3, lwd = 2)
legend("topright", c("Observed values (y = 0)", "Kernel for highlighted value", "Sum = KDE"),
       col = c("black", orange, blue), lty = c(NA, 1, 1),
       pch = c(16, NA, NA), lwd = c(NA, 2, 3), bty = "n", cex = .85)
```

**Read the alignment.** The normal kernel centred at observation $X_i$ has mean, median, and **mode at $x=X_i$**. The point $(X_i,0)$ lies directly below that kernel's peak. Scaling the kernel by $1/n$ changes its height and area but does not move its mode. The observation is plotted on the baseline to mark its location; its plotted height is not its estimated density.

The highlighted point and peak therefore share the same horizontal coordinate. An observed value need not be a mode of the **sum**: overlapping kernels can shift the modes of the final KDE.


Every contribution has area $1/n$, so the full estimate integrates to one. Larger $h$ means wider and lower individual bumps, not additional observations.

**Check understanding.** If we double the sample by repeating every observation exactly once and keep $h$ fixed, the KDE does not change. Replication does not add new information about the population.

## Density is not probability at a point

For a continuous distribution, probability is area over an interval. A density height can exceed one and changes when measurement units change. For $Z=aX+b$, $a>0$, the corresponding bandwidth is $h_Z=ah_X$, and

\[
\widehat f_Z(z)=\frac1a\widehat f_X\!\left(\frac{z-b}{a}\right).
\]

```{r probability-area}
# Gaussian-kernel interval probability: integrate each component exactly.
a <- -.5
b <- 1
estimated_probability <- mean(pnorm((b - x_small) / h_small) -
                               pnorm((a - x_small) / h_small))
c(KDE_interval_probability = estimated_probability,
  Empirical_interval_proportion = mean(x_small >= a & x_small <= b))
```

These two numbers need not agree: one uses a smoothed empirical distribution, the other uses the empirical distribution directly.

## Activity 1: units and probability

Use these **simulated durations in seconds**, supplied specifically for this
activity. They are separate from the dimensionless observations `x_small`.

```{r activity-1-data}
duration_seconds <- c(25, 35, 48, 60, 74, 90, 110, 135)
h_seconds <- 12
grid_seconds <- seq(0, 180, length.out = 501)
density_seconds <- kde(duration_seconds, grid_seconds, h_seconds)
```

Predict the equivalent bandwidth in minutes and the change in density
height. Compute a second KDE using `duration_seconds / 60`,
`grid_seconds / 60`, and your bandwidth in minutes. Convert that curve back
to seconds before overlaying it on `density_seconds`. Submit the plot and
check that the estimated probability between 30 and 90 seconds equals the
probability between 0.5 and 1.5 minutes. Explain why probability is unchanged
even though the numerical density heights change.

# Bandwidth changes the scientific story

## Start with real waiting times

The built-in `datasets::faithful` dataset records 272 eruptions of the Old
Faithful geyser in Yellowstone. Each row is one recorded eruption;
`eruptions` is its duration and `waiting` is the waiting time to the next
eruption, both in minutes. These are real observations, not simulated mixture
components. See [`?faithful`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/datasets/html/faithful.html)
for the source and measurement notes. The data
contain rounded measurements; do not interpret fine-scale spikes as precision
the observations do not have. Consecutive observations may be dependent, so
this descriptive example is not evidence for an independent sampling model.

We need a starting bandwidth before drawing a curve. **`bw.SJ()` is the
Sheather-Jones bandwidth selector**: it returns one positive number, in the
same units as the observations. Its intuition is to balance two problems:
too little smoothing leaves a noisy curve, while too much smoothing hides
features. It first uses preliminary smooth estimates to assess how strongly
the density bends, then uses that information and the sample size to choose
a bandwidth. It estimates the unknown curvature rather than assuming we
already know the population density.

This is a starting resolution, not a guarantee that every peak is real.
Here we also inspect half and twice that bandwidth. The later section
[Automatic selectors are starting points](#bandwidth-selectors-explained)
explains the rule of thumb and the Sheather-Jones idea in more detail.

```{r faithful-data}
waiting <- datasets::faithful$waiting
h_wait <- bw.SJ(waiting)
g_wait <- seq(min(waiting) - 15, max(waiting) + 15, length.out = 501)
wait_adjust <- c(.5, 1, 2)
wait_curves <- sapply(wait_adjust, function(a)
  kde(waiting, g_wait, a * h_wait))
```

## Activity 2: how many peaks would you report?

Before running the next chunk, predict what halving or doubling the bandwidth
will do. Use the same data and axes in all three panels. Report one broad
feature that persists and one detail that changes. Include the units, sample
size, and bandwidth in your explanation. Does a peak prove that there is a
distinct latent population group?

```{r faithful-bandwidth-panels, fig.width=10, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="The same real waiting times at three smoothing resolutions. There is no known population density to overlay."}
with_panels(1, 3, {
  for (j in seq_along(wait_adjust)) {
    hist(waiting, breaks = seq(40, 100, by = 5), probability = TRUE,
         xlim = range(g_wait), ylim = c(0, max(wait_curves) * 1.1),
         col = "grey90", border = "white", xlab = "Waiting time (minutes)",
         main = paste0("h = ", round(wait_adjust[j] * h_wait, 2), " minutes"))
    lines(g_wait, wait_curves[, j], col = blue, lwd = 2)
    rug(waiting, col = adjustcolor("black", .2))
  }
})
```

## One sample, several resolutions

We simulate a two-component population so that the truth is known. In real data, we do not have this reference curve.

```{r mixture-data}
r_mix <- function(n) {
  component <- rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = .45)
  rnorm(n, mean = ifelse(component == 0, -1.2, 1.3),
        sd = ifelse(component == 0, .6, .45))
}
f_mix <- function(z) .55 * dnorm(z, -1.2, .6) + .45 * dnorm(z, 1.3, .45)
set.seed(1101)
x <- r_mix(220)
grid <- seq(-4.5, 4.5, length.out = 501)
h_values <- c(.10, .35, 1.10)
estimates <- sapply(h_values, function(h) kde(x, grid, h))
```

```{r bandwidth-panels, fig.width=10, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="The same sample and axis limits are used in all panels; the dashed curve is the generating density.", fig.alt="Small bandwidth produces many peaks; a moderate bandwidth reveals two groups; a large bandwidth merges their detail."}
with_panels(1, 3, {
  for (j in seq_along(h_values)) {
    plot(grid, estimates[, j], type = "l", col = blue, lwd = 2,
         ylim = c(0, max(estimates, f_mix(grid)) * 1.05),
         xlab = "x", ylab = "Density", main = paste("h =", h_values[j]))
    lines(grid, f_mix(grid), lty = 2, lwd = 2)
    rug(x, col = adjustcolor("black", .25))
  }
})
```

Count the apparent peaks in each panel and compare them with the generating
density. A wiggle is not automatically a population subgroup. Conversely, a
smooth unimodal curve can conceal a genuinely multimodal population.

We deliberately show a broad range of bandwidths. The middle value is illustrative, not a universal recommendation.

## Histogram and KDE on a compatible scale

```{r histogram-overlay, fig.cap="A density-scaled histogram and KDE share the same vertical units."}
hist(x, breaks = seq(-5, 5, by = .4), probability = TRUE,
     col = "grey90", border = "white", xlab = "x", main = "Density, not counts")
lines(grid, kde(x, grid, .35), col = blue, lwd = 2)
rug(x, col = adjustcolor("black", .3))
```

Bin width and bandwidth both control resolution, but they define different estimators. A numerical bin width of 0.4 is not equivalent to a Gaussian bandwidth of 0.4.

# Sample size: more observations at a fixed bandwidth

## Keep the smoothing parameter unchanged

Now change **only the sample size**. Draw one large independent sample from a standard normal population and use nested prefixes of sizes 30, 150, 750, and 3750. Every panel uses the same Gaussian bandwidth $h=0.18$, evaluation grid, and axis limits.

With more observations, the random gaps and clusters average out: the estimated curve generally looks **less irregular and more stable**, although we have not widened the kernels. A particular sequence of samples need not become monotonically less wiggly at every step.

```{r fixed-bandwidth-sample-size, fig.width=9, fig.height=7, fig.cap="Increasing sample size at the same bandwidth h = 0.18. Blue: estimated KDE; dashed black: true density; dotted orange: the fixed-bandwidth expected density.", fig.alt="Four nested samples increase from 30 to 3750 observations. Their density estimates become more stable at a fixed Gaussian bandwidth."}
set.seed(1104)
sample_sizes <- c(30, 150, 750, 3750)
h_fixed <- .18
x_pool <- rnorm(max(sample_sizes))
g_n <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 601)
curves_n <- sapply(sample_sizes, function(n)
  kde(x_pool[seq_len(n)], g_n, h_fixed))
truth_n <- dnorm(g_n)
# Convolving N(0,1) with N(0,h^2) gives N(0,1+h^2).
expected_n <- dnorm(g_n, sd = sqrt(1 + h_fixed^2))
common_ylim <- c(-.015, 1.18 * max(curves_n, truth_n, expected_n))
with_panels(2, 2, {
  for (j in seq_along(sample_sizes)) {
    n_j <- sample_sizes[j]
    plot(g_n, curves_n[, j], type = "l", col = blue, lwd = 2,
         xlim = range(g_n), ylim = common_ylim,
         xlab = "x", ylab = "Density",
         main = paste0("n = ", n_j, "; h = ", h_fixed))
    lines(g_n, truth_n, lty = 2, lwd = 1.7)
    lines(g_n, expected_n, col = orange, lty = 3, lwd = 1.7)
    abline(h = 0, col = "grey85")
    points(x_pool[seq_len(n_j)], rep(0, n_j), pch = "|",
           col = adjustcolor("black", .18), cex = .55)
    if (j == 1) legend("topright", c("KDE", "Truth", "Expected KDE"),
                       col = c(blue, "black", orange), lty = c(1, 2, 3),
                       lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = .7)
  }
})
```

**Discussion questions.** Which peaks persist as new observations are added? Is the kernel width changing? Does the larger sample make the curve more Gaussian because we assumed normal kernels, or because this particular population is normal?

Here the population is normal by construction. Repeating the experiment with a bimodal population would stabilise its smoothed bimodal shape, not force the estimate into one normal curve.

## Activity 3: distinguish more data from more smoothing

Generate a nested normal sample of sizes 80, 800, and 8000. Compare bandwidths
0.08, 0.25, and 0.7, holding each bandwidth fixed as sample size changes.
Repeat for several seeds, keep identical axes and the true density visible,
and report which sample-specific peaks persist. Explain why a bandwidth
suited to 80 observations need not be suited to 8000. Replicating the same
observations is not the same experiment as collecting new observations.

## What decreases, and what remains?

At a fixed evaluation point $x$, let $Z_i=K_h(x-X_i)$. Independent sampling gives

\[
\widehat f_h(x)=\frac1n\sum_i Z_i,
\qquad \operatorname{Var}\{\widehat f_h(x)\}
=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(Z_i)}{n}.
\]

At **fixed $h$**, increasing $n$ by a factor of five reduces pointwise variance by a factor of five, and standard deviation by $\sqrt{5}$. It does not remove smoothing bias: the expectation is the same convolution $f*K_h$ for every $n$.

For this example, that expectation is a normal density with variance $1+h^2$, slightly wider than the generating $N(0,1)$ density. The orange and black curves nearly overlap because $h=0.18$ is small; their difference does not shrink just because $n$ increases.

```{r sample-size-variability}
# Exact pointwise standard deviation at x = 0 for this normal example.
mean_z <- dnorm(0, sd = sqrt(1 + h_fixed^2))
second_moment_z <- dnorm(0, sd = sqrt(1 + h_fixed^2 / 2)) /
  (2 * sqrt(pi) * h_fixed)
variance_z <- second_moment_z - mean_z^2
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  sample_size = sample_sizes,
  bandwidth = h_fixed,
  expected_density_at_zero = mean_z,
  bias_at_zero = mean_z - dnorm(0),
  standard_deviation_at_zero = sqrt(variance_z / sample_sizes)
), digits = 5)
```

“More smooth” here refers to reduced sample-specific irregularity. Every Gaussian KDE is already differentiable to all orders, even with very few observations. For consistency for the unsmoothed density, one usually lets $h$ decrease as $n$ grows, with $nh$ increasing; that is a different experiment from holding $h$ fixed.

# Bias and variance: examine repeated samples

## What changes when another sample is collected?

A small bandwidth makes the estimate sensitive to the particular observations. A large bandwidth averages over a wider neighbourhood, reducing sampling variability but blurring structure. Bias refers to the difference between the **average estimate over repeated samples** and the true density, not to every discrepancy in one curve.

```{r kde-monte-carlo}
set.seed(1102)
mc_grid <- seq(-4.5, 4.5, length.out = 301)
mc_est <- array(NA_real_, dim = c(length(mc_grid), B, length(h_values)))
for (b in seq_len(B)) {
  xb <- r_mix(220)
  for (j in seq_along(h_values)) {
    mc_est[, b, j] <- kde(xb, mc_grid, h_values[j])
  }
}
# Exact mean of the Gaussian KDE for this Gaussian mixture:
# convolution adds the kernel variance h^2 to each component variance.
expected_kde <- function(z, h) {
  .55 * dnorm(z, -1.2, sqrt(.6^2 + h^2)) +
    .45 * dnorm(z, 1.3, sqrt(.45^2 + h^2))
}
```

```{r repeated-curves, fig.width=10, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Thin lines are estimates from repeated samples; blue is the exact expected estimate; black dashed is the truth.", fig.alt="Repeated small-bandwidth estimates vary strongly; large-bandwidth estimates vary less but systematically blur the two modes."}
with_panels(1, 3, {
  for (j in seq_along(h_values)) {
    matplot(mc_grid, mc_est[, seq_len(min(B, 20)), j], type = "l", lty = 1,
            col = adjustcolor("grey40", .25), ylim = c(0, max(mc_est)),
            main = paste("h =", h_values[j]), xlab = "x", ylab = "Density")
    lines(mc_grid, expected_kde(mc_grid, h_values[j]), col = blue, lwd = 3)
    lines(mc_grid, f_mix(mc_grid), lty = 2, lwd = 2)
  }
})
```

## Quantify the trade-off

At a fixed $x$,

\[
E\{[\widehat f_h(x)-f(x)]^2\}
=\operatorname{Var}\{\widehat f_h(x)\}
 +[E\{\widehat f_h(x)\}-f(x)]^2.
\]

Integrate this identity over $x$ to obtain the corresponding decomposition of mean integrated squared error (MISE). Here we approximate the integrals on a fine grid and estimate the variance by simulation.

```{r bias-variance-table}
tradeoff <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(h_values), function(j) {
  bias <- expected_kde(mc_grid, h_values[j]) - f_mix(mc_grid)
  integrated_bias2 <- trapz(mc_grid, bias^2)
  integrated_variance <- trapz(mc_grid, apply(mc_est[, , j], 1, var))
  empirical_mise <- mean(apply(mc_est[, , j], 2, function(est)
    trapz(mc_grid, (est - f_mix(mc_grid))^2)))
  data.frame(h = h_values[j], integrated_bias2, integrated_variance,
             sum_components = integrated_bias2 + integrated_variance,
             empirical_mise)
}))
knitr::kable(tradeoff, digits = 5)
```

The last two columns are close, not necessarily identical, because a finite number of simulated samples is used. They also refer to the finite integration interval. Increase `simulation_reps` to reduce Monte Carlo error.

## Activity 4: read repeated curves before the error table

Compare the thin curves with the expected KDE and the true density. Which
bandwidth gives the largest variability? Which most strongly blurs the two
modes? Write two sentences distinguishing sampling variability from smoothing
bias, then use the table to support them. Explain why increasing simulation
repetitions is different from increasing the size of each sample.

## Optional theory: why sample size matters

For independent observations, a sufficiently smooth density, a symmetric second-order kernel, and an interior point, the leading terms behave as

\[
\operatorname{Bias}(\widehat f_h(x))\approx
\tfrac12 h^2\mu_2(K)f''(x),\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat f_h(x))\approx\frac{f(x)R(K)}{nh},
\]

where $\mu_2(K)=\int u^2K(u)\,du$ and $R(K)=\int K(u)^2\,du$.
The integrated approximation has the form $C_1h^4+C_2/(nh)$ with positive constants under the usual nondegeneracy conditions. Balancing the two terms gives

\[
h_{\mathrm{AMISE}}\propto n^{-1/5}.
\]

Thus, multiplying the sample size by 32 allows a bandwidth roughly half as large under these assumptions. This is an asymptotic rate, not a universal finite-sample choice, and boundary points require separate treatment. The constants depend on the density and the kernel.

# Choosing a bandwidth in practice

## Automatic selectors are starting points {#bandwidth-selectors-explained}

For ordinary nondegenerate samples, R's `bw.nrd0` uses

\[
h=0.9\min\{s,\operatorname{IQR}/1.34\}\,n^{-1/5},
\]

Here $s$ is the sample standard deviation and $n$ is the sample size. The
minimum of $s$ and $\operatorname{IQR}/1.34$ estimates spread while reducing
the influence of extreme observations. The $n^{-1/5}$ factor makes the chosen
bandwidth smaller as more observations become available. R includes fallback
rules when the estimated spread is zero. This is a normal-reference rule,
not an optimum for every distribution.

**How does `bw.SJ` improve on this?** Spread alone does not describe the
shape of a density: two distributions with similar spread may have very
different peaks and valleys. Sheather-Jones uses preliminary estimates of
density derivatives to estimate curvature. The second derivative $f''(x)$
measures how strongly the curve bends: smoothing across a sharp bend can
introduce more bias than smoothing a nearly straight part.

The theoretical balance has the form
$C_1h^4+C_2/(nh)$: the first part grows with excessive smoothing and depends
on curvature; the second part reflects sampling variability and decreases
with smoothing. A **pilot estimate** is a preliminary smooth estimate used
to estimate the unknown quantities in this balance. **Plug-in** means
replacing those unknown quantities with estimates from the observations.
In R, `bw.SJ()` defaults to a solve-the-equation version (`method = "ste"`);
`method = "dpi"` requests the direct plug-in version. You do not need the
algorithm's derivation to interpret the returned bandwidth or to check its
sensitivity with `adjust`.

`bw.ucv` instead compares bandwidths through a leave-one-out criterion, as
explained in the next optional section. All these automatic choices are
starting points; they can disagree, especially for small or multimodal
samples. These selectors are designed for Gaussian KDEs. In the later kernel
comparison we deliberately keep one bandwidth fixed to compare shapes,
rather than optimise a separate bandwidth for each kernel. See the
[R documentation for bandwidth selectors](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/bandwidth.html).

```{r bandwidth-selectors}
h_auto <- c(nrd0 = bw.nrd0(waiting), SJ = bw.SJ(waiting))
knitr::kable(data.frame(selector = names(h_auto), bandwidth = unname(h_auto)),
             digits = 4)
# density() uses bw = "nrd0" by default.
d_default <- density(waiting)
d_sj <- density(waiting, bw = "SJ")
# adjust multiplies the selected bandwidth:
d_half <- density(waiting, bw = "SJ", adjust = .5)
```

```{r selector-plot, fig.cap="Automatic bandwidth choices for real waiting times; neither is validated by a known population density."}
plot(d_default, col = blue, lwd = 2, ylim = c(0, max(d_default$y, d_sj$y)),
     xlab = "Waiting time (minutes)", main = "Two starting resolutions")
lines(d_sj, col = orange, lwd = 2)
rug(waiting, col = adjustcolor("black", .2))
legend("topright", c("nrd0", "SJ"),
       col = c(blue, orange), lty = 1, lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

**Practical workflow:** select a defensible starting value; show a small range around it; retain raw observations or a histogram; describe features that persist. When comparing groups on the same measurement scale, consider using a common bandwidth to compare at a common resolution. A common bandwidth is not necessarily optimal for each group.

Changing `density(..., n = 2048)` increases the number of evaluation points; it does **not** replace the bandwidth as the smoothing parameter.

## Activity 5: bandwidth selection is a starting point

For `faithful$eruptions`, compare `bw.nrd0` and `bw.SJ`. Plot 0.5, 1, and 2
times the SJ bandwidth on identical axes, with a rug and duration in minutes.
Submit the plot and a short account of the stable features. Explain why
changing `density(..., n = 2048)` answers a different question from changing

## Optional: least-squares cross-validation for KDE

For a realised sample, integrated squared error is

\[
\operatorname{ISE}(h)=\int\widehat f_h^2(x)\,dx
-2\int\widehat f_h(x)f(x)\,dx+\int f^2(x)\,dx.
\]

The last term does not depend on $h$. We estimate the second term using leave-one-out densities:

\[
\operatorname{CV}(h)=\int\widehat f_h^2(x)\,dx
-\frac2n\sum_i\widehat f_{h,-i}(X_i).
\]

Leaving observation $i$ out prevents its own kernel from inflating the density evaluated at $X_i$. Under independent sampling this criterion estimates the relevant integrated risk up to an additive constant. It targets integrated density error.

For Gaussian kernels the first integral is available analytically. The next implementation evaluates the criterion on a candidate grid, without numerical integration.

```{r kde-cv}
gaussian_lscv <- function(x, h) {
  n <- length(x)
  delta <- outer(x, x, "-")
  int_f2 <- mean(dnorm(delta, sd = sqrt(2) * h))
  leave_out <- dnorm(delta, sd = h)
  diag(leave_out) <- 0
  int_ff <- sum(leave_out) / (n * (n - 1))
  int_f2 - 2 * int_ff
}
h_grid <- exp(seq(log(.07), log(1.2), length.out = 65))
cv_kde <- vapply(h_grid, function(h) gaussian_lscv(x, h), numeric(1))
h_cv <- h_grid[which.min(cv_kde)]
# Oracle comparison: possible only because this is a simulation.
ise <- vapply(h_grid, function(h)
  trapz(grid, (kde(x, grid, h) - f_mix(grid))^2), numeric(1))
h_oracle <- h_grid[which.min(ise)]
knitr::kable(data.frame(method = c("CV grid minimum", "Realised-sample oracle"),
                       bandwidth = c(h_cv, h_oracle)), digits = 4)
```

```{r kde-cv-plot, fig.width=9, fig.height=4, fig.cap="CV is observable; the realised-sample ISE is an oracle quantity available only in simulation."}
with_panels(1, 2, {
  plot(h_grid, cv_kde, type = "l", log = "x", lwd = 2, col = blue,
       xlab = "Bandwidth (log axis)", ylab = "LSCV criterion")
  abline(v = h_cv, lty = 2)
  plot(h_grid, ise, type = "l", log = "x", lwd = 2, col = orange,
       xlab = "Bandwidth (log axis)", ylab = "Integrated squared error")
  abline(v = h_oracle, lty = 2)
})
```

The selected bandwidths need not coincide. The oracle minimises error for this particular sample, while CV is a noisy risk estimate. The grid is part of the procedure: if its minimum is at an endpoint, expand it and inspect the criterion. Different numerical searches need not return exactly the same result as this grid.

## Kernel shape versus bandwidth

The Gaussian is convenient, but it is not the only kernel. In general,

\[
\widehat f_h(x)=\frac{1}{nh}\sum_{i=1}^n K\!\left(\frac{x-X_i}{h}\right).
\]

For the nonnegative kernels considered here, each contribution still has area
$1/n$. Changing $K$ changes the shape of each contribution; changing $h$
changes its scale. A rectangular kernel has a flat top, so the earlier
statement about a unique peak at each observation applies to the Gaussian,
not to every kernel.

| Kernel | Shape and support | What to notice |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Gaussian | Smooth bell; infinite support | Nonzero tails extend beyond every observation. |
| Epanechnikov | Parabolic bump; compact support | A common efficient second-order kernel; not universally best in finite samples. |
| Triangular | Piecewise linear bump; compact support | A pointed peak and finite neighbourhood. |
| Rectangular | Flat bump; compact support | Abrupt edges can produce a visibly less smooth estimate. |

R also offers `biweight`, `cosine`, and `optcosine`. Its `density()` function
rescales all these kernels to variance one: `bw` is the standard deviation
of the smoothing kernel. A textbook Epanechnikov kernel on [-1, 1] uses a
different scaling convention. Equal `bw` gives equal kernel standard
deviations, not identical support widths or exactly equal risk. See the
[R documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/density.html).

```{r kernel-shapes, fig.cap="Individual kernels centred at zero, with bandwidth 1 under R's unit-variance convention."}
kernel_names <- c("gaussian", "epanechnikov", "triangular", "rectangular")
kernel_colours <- c(blue, orange, green, purple)
kernel_shapes <- lapply(kernel_names, function(k)
  density(0, bw = 1, kernel = k, from = -4, to = 4, n = 1024))
plot(kernel_shapes[[1]], col = blue, lwd = 2,
     ylim = c(0, max(vapply(kernel_shapes, function(d) max(d$y), numeric(1)))),
     xlab = "Distance from the observation", main = "Same standard deviation")
for (j in 2:length(kernel_names)) {
  lines(kernel_shapes[[j]], col = kernel_colours[j], lty = j, lwd = 2)
}
legend("topright", kernel_names, col = kernel_colours,
       lty = seq_along(kernel_names), lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = .8)
```

## Activity 6: kernel or bandwidth?

Use the same waiting times, the same evaluation grid, and `bw = h_wait`.
Compare the four kernels below. Then repeat with `bw = 2 * h_wait` while
holding the kernel Gaussian. Which change affects the broad interpretation
more? Report persistent features and local differences; do not select a
kernel solely because it gives the desired number of peaks.

```{r kernels, fig.cap="Four kernels applied to real waiting times at a common kernel standard deviation. The bandwidth has been fixed before comparing shapes."}
kernel_estimates <- lapply(kernel_names, function(k)
  density(waiting, bw = h_wait, kernel = k, from = min(g_wait),
          to = max(g_wait), n = 1024))
plot(kernel_estimates[[1]], col = blue, lwd = 2,
     ylim = c(0, max(vapply(kernel_estimates, function(d) max(d$y), numeric(1)))),
     xlab = "Waiting time (minutes)", main = "Kernel shape at a fixed scale")
for (j in 2:length(kernel_names)) {
  lines(kernel_estimates[[j]], col = kernel_colours[j], lty = 1, lwd = 2)
}
rug(waiting, col = adjustcolor("black", .2))
legend("topright", kernel_names, col = kernel_colours,
       lty = 1, lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = .8)
```

For many ordinary KDE comparisons, bandwidth changes the broad shape more
than switching between common kernels at comparable scales. Kernel choice
still affects support and smoothness. A compact-support kernel does not
automatically solve a boundary problem: its bump can cross zero when an
observation is near zero. The earlier exact convolution and cross-validation
formulas remain specifically Gaussian; do not reuse them unchanged for other
kernels.

# Boundary problems: smoothness cannot override support

A Gaussian KDE of a positive variable assigns some probability to negative values. Hiding that part of the curve changes the display but does not correct the estimator.

One alternative is to estimate the density of $Z=\log X$, then express that
density in the original units. **Changing the horizontal axis alone is not
enough**, because density means probability *per unit of horizontal length*.
The logarithm compresses larger values more strongly than smaller values.
The height must change as well to preserve probability as area.

For a small interval of width $dx$ near $x>0$, the corresponding interval on
the log scale has width approximately $dz=dx/x$, since
$d\log(x)/dx=1/x$. The same probability can be written on either scale:

\[
f_X(x)\,dx \approx f_Z(\log x)\,dz
             \approx f_Z(\log x)\frac{dx}{x}.
\]

Consequently, the change-of-variable formula is

\[
\widehat f_X(x)=\frac{\widehat f_Z(\log x)}{x},\qquad x>0.
\]

The factor $1/x$ is the absolute derivative of the transformation. In one
dimension this is called the **Jacobian factor**. Here it simply converts
density per log-unit into density per original unit. For example, an interval
of one mile near 100 miles corresponds to about 0.01 log-units: its probability
is approximately $\widehat f_Z(\log 100)\times0.01$, so its density per mile
is approximately $\widehat f_Z(\log 100)/100$.

In code, evaluate the log-scale KDE at `log(grid_original)`, then divide its
heights by `grid_original`. Exponentiating the log coordinates without dividing
the heights by $x$ would not preserve the area or produce a density in the
original units.

```{r boundary-example, fig.cap="Ordinary KDE leaks below zero. A log-scale estimator respects positivity but still has estimation error."}
set.seed(1103)
positive <- rlnorm(250, meanlog = 0, sdlog = .65)
g_pos <- seq(-1, 5, length.out = 601)
h_pos <- bw.SJ(positive)
ordinary <- kde(positive, g_pos, h_pos)
# Fit on log values; division by x converts heights to original-scale density.
g_strict <- seq(.015, 5, length.out = 601)
h_log <- bw.SJ(log(positive))
log_corrected <- kde(log(positive), log(g_strict), h_log) / g_strict
plot(g_pos, ordinary, type = "l", col = blue, lwd = 2,
     ylim = c(0, max(ordinary, log_corrected, dlnorm(g_strict, 0, .65))),
     xlab = "Positive variable", ylab = "Density", main = "Respect the support")
lines(g_strict, log_corrected, col = orange, lwd = 2)
lines(g_strict, dlnorm(g_strict, 0, .65), lty = 2, lwd = 2)
abline(v = 0, col = "grey50")
rug(positive, col = adjustcolor("black", .25))
legend("topright", c("Ordinary KDE", "Log-transform KDE", "Truth"),
       col = c(blue, orange, "black"), lty = c(1, 1, 2), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
mean(pnorm(-positive / h_pos))  # exact mass below zero for ordinary KDE
```

The $1/x$ factor is essential. This transformation is not available for zero
or negative observations without a different model, and it changes the
smoothing scale: smoothing on the log scale is multiplicative on the original
scale. It is one approach, not a universal boundary correction.

## Activity 7: check support on real measurements

The built-in `datasets::rivers` dataset contains lengths in miles of 141 major
North American rivers; one observation is one river. Consult
[`?rivers`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/datasets/html/rivers.html)
for the source. This is a collection of major rivers, not a random sample of all rivers.
Compare an ordinary Gaussian KDE with a KDE fitted to log lengths. Express
the latter in miles using the formula just derived: evaluate at the log of
each positive grid value and divide the density by that grid value. Submit
a plot with units and compute the
ordinary KDE's mass below zero. Discuss the support problem and the effect of
the changed smoothing scale; do not claim that the corrected curve is truth.

```{r rivers-support}
river_lengths <- datasets::rivers
h_river <- bw.SJ(river_lengths)
g_river <- seq(-500, max(river_lengths) + 500, length.out = 801)
g_river_positive <- seq(1, max(river_lengths) + 500, length.out = 801)
ordinary_river <- kde(river_lengths, g_river, h_river)
log_river <- kde(log(river_lengths), log(g_river_positive),
                 bw.SJ(log(river_lengths))) / g_river_positive
plot(g_river, ordinary_river, type = "l", col = blue, lwd = 2,
     ylim = c(0, max(ordinary_river, log_river)),
     xlab = "River length (miles)", ylab = "Density", main = "Physical support")
lines(g_river_positive, log_river, col = orange, lwd = 2)
abline(v = 0, lty = 2)
rug(river_lengths, col = adjustcolor("black", .2))
legend("topright", c("Ordinary KDE", "Log-transform KDE"),
       col = c(blue, orange), lty = 1, lwd = 2, bty = "n")
mean(pnorm(-river_lengths / h_river))
```
